title: Making peace with your story
hook: finding God even in the chapters you'd delete

segments.voice: Yesterday, courage: Joshua and Esther, afraid and going anyway. Your line was brave enough.

If your life were a book, which chapter would you tear out? The thing you did, or the thing that was done to you. Some people carry a page like that, folded small. The Bible has a man with chapters he'd have every right to tear out: thrown in a pit by his brothers, sold as a slave, falsely accused, forgotten in prison. At the end of his story, he says something about those chapters to the very brothers who wrote them.

Joseph's jealous brothers strip off his coat, throw him in a pit, and sell him to traders bound for Egypt. There he's a slave, falsely accused, left in prison. Years later he runs Egypt's grain stores, and in a famine his brothers come to buy grain, not knowing him. There's a tearful reunion. But today's scene comes after their father Jacob dies. The brothers panic: now he'll pay us back. They send word asking forgiveness, and Joseph weeps. Then they fall down before him, and he says, in the King James words: "Fear not: for am I in the place of God? But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive." Joseph doesn't call the pit good. He calls it evil, plainly. But he says God was at work in the same chapter, bending it toward saving lives. That's making peace with your story here: not pretending a hard chapter didn't happen, not tearing it out, but letting God hold it. The prophet Joel, after locusts strip the land, hears God promise: "I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten." And a psalm says even dark chapters aren't hidden: "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." Christians explain how God works in suffering in different ways, and some are wary of easy answers. But in Genesis, even the pit is inside the story God is telling.

segments.voice: Choose one chapter you'd rather delete, not the worst if that's too much today, and see it plainly, the way Joseph named evil as evil. Then gently ask whether anything grew after it, knowing you don't have to find one; if you pray, bring it to God with Joel's line, I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten. If a hard chapter is still happening and you're not safe, please reach local emergency help, or in the US call or text 988.
Making peace with your story. In Joseph's words, naming the evil honestly, and trusting that God was at work in the same chapter.

howItsDone: Christians bring the hard parts of their lives to God in prayer, confession, counseling and spiritual direction, and some practice a prayerful review of the day or of their life, looking for where God was present.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. your father has died, and the brothers who sold you into slavery are on their knees, afraid you'll finally pay them back. what do you do?
options: take your revenge now that your father is gone.
weep, tell them fear not, and promise to care for them.
send them away and never see them again.
fork.reveal: Joseph weeps and says, fear not: for am I in the place of God? ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good. then he promises to nourish them and their little ones.

chat.says: Does making peace with my past mean saying what happened to me was okay?
options: No. Joseph calls what his brothers did evil, yet says God meant it unto good.
Yes. Joseph tells his brothers the pit was really a good thing all along.
Yes. Joseph makes peace by acting as if his brothers had never hurt him.
chat.meaning: In Genesis 50:20 Joseph says, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good. He names the wrong plainly and still sees God at work.

Joseph.meaning: Jacob's son, sold by his brothers, who rose in Egypt

Joseph's coat (Genesis 37:23) is mentioned without 'of many colours' to avoid the KJV/Hebrew translation question.
The teach avoids Romans 8:28 and any claim that suffering is good in itself; confirm the balance ('Christians don't all explain how God works in suffering').
